Conflation is the act of merging two or more separate, distinct things together and treating them as if they are one and the same — when in reality, they are different and should be kept apart.

Think of it this way: imagine you have two puzzle pieces from two different puzzles. They look somewhat similar, so you force them together and call them one piece. That forcing-together — that mistaken merging — is conflation.

The "things" being merged can be ideas, arguments, concepts, words, events, groups of people, or categories. Almost any kind of thing can be conflated with another.
Why It's Almost Always a Problem

Conflation is typically considered an error in thinking or communication — sometimes an honest mistake, sometimes a deliberate trick to mislead.

The problem is this: when you treat two different things as one, you lose the important distinctions between them. And those distinctions matter. Decisions, arguments, and conclusions built on a conflation are therefore flawed at the root, because they rest on a false foundation — the false idea that Thing A and Thing B are the same when they aren't.

This is why you'll most often hear the word "conflation" used as a criticism. When someone says "that's a conflation," they are pointing out that the person being criticized has illegitimately merged two things that need to be treated separately.

Conflation almost always happens because two things genuinely do share something in common — they overlap, they're related, or they resemble each other in some way. That partial similarity is what causes (or enables) the mistake.

But sharing something in common does not make two things the same. Conflation is the error of jumping from "these two things are related / similar" to "these two things are identical / interchangeable."

Consider: a square and a rectangle are related — every square is a rectangle. But if you conflated them and said "every rectangle is a square," you'd be wrong. The relationship is real, but the identity is false.

Example 1 — Conflating criticism of a government with hatred of a people

Criticising the government of a country is not the same as hating the people of that country. These are two distinct things. If someone says, "You criticised our government, so you must hate us," they are conflating political criticism with hatred of a group. The two can overlap, but they are not the same, and treating them as though they are is a conflation.

Example 2 — Conflating correlation with causation

Suppose ice cream sales and drowning incidents both rise during summer. Someone might say, "Ice cream causes drowning!" But correlation (two things happening at the same time) is not the same as causation (one thing causing the other). Conflating these two — treating "they happen together" as "one causes the other" — is one of the most common logical errors humans make.

Example 3 — Conflating price with value

Something expensive is not automatically valuable, and something cheap is not automatically worthless. Price and value are related but different concepts. If someone says, "This must be great — it costs a fortune," they are conflating price with value.

Example 4 — Conflating a person's identity with their behaviour

"You made a mistake, therefore you are a mistake" — this conflates a specific action a person did with their entire identity as a person. The action and the person are distinct; the action can be judged without defining the whole person.

Example 5 — Conflating two words that seem similar

People often conflate "jealousy" and "envy." Envy is wanting something someone else has. Jealousy is the fear of losing something you already have (like a relationship). These feel similar, but they are psychologically distinct states. Using them interchangeably is conflation.

Not all conflation is an innocent mistake. Sometimes people conflate things on purpose to manipulate an argument or mislead an audience. This is a rhetorical trick.

For example, a politician might conflate "reducing the military budget" with "leaving the country defenceless" — these are not the same thing (a smaller budget does not automatically mean no defence), but merging them makes the opponent's position sound extreme and dangerous.

When conflation is deliberate, it functions as a form of dishonest argumentation — creating a false impression by blurring real distinctions.

It's worth being clear about what does not count as conflation, so the concept stays sharp.

Comparison is not conflation. You can compare two things — noting their similarities and differences — while keeping them perfectly separate. Conflation happens when the separation disappears entirely and the two things get treated as one.

Legitimate synthesis is not conflation. In academic or creative work, sometimes two ideas genuinely do belong together and can be meaningfully unified. That careful, justified merging is not conflation — it's synthesis. Conflation is the unjustified or careless version of this.

Overlap is not conflation. Two things can genuinely share common ground without being the same. Noting that overlap correctly is fine. Conflation only occurs when you stop there and declare the two things identical.
How to Spot Conflation in the Wild

You'll most commonly encounter this word when someone — a commentator, a writer, a thinker — identifies a flaw in another person's reasoning. The tell-tale signs that conflation is happening include:

When two very different things are spoken about as if they are automatically interchangeable. When an argument quietly slides from one concept to another without acknowledging the difference. When saying "that's not the same thing" would immediately break the argument apart.

If you hear someone say "you're conflating two very different things," what they mean is: "Your argument only works if these two things are the same — but they're not, and treating them as if they are is the mistake at the heart of your reasoning."

Conflation is the act of illegitimately erasing a real and important distinction between two things, and treating what is actually two as if it is one. It is almost always a flaw — in thinking, in argument, or in communication. Recognising conflation (in others' arguments and in your own thinking) is one of the sharpest tools you can develop for clear reasoning.
